name: Han China
title: Social Hierarchy of Han China: From Emperor to Enslaved
period: 206 BCE – 220 CE (the Western and Eastern Han)

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You are the Son of Heaven, whose name no subject may speak and who alone makes and repeals the laws, but if you come to the throne as a child, your mother’s family may rule in your name.
tiers.kid: The Han emperor was called the Son of Heaven, and people were not allowed to say his name.
tiers.rise: The throne passed to the son the emperor named heir apparent or, failing one, to a prince the empress dowager chose. Liu Bang himself had been a commoner who rose in the revolts against the Qin.
tiers.why: The emperor (huangdi), the Son of Heaven (tianzi), was always a man of the Liu family descended from the founder, Liu Bang.

tiers.name: Kings and marquesses
tiers.you: You are a king of the Liu clan, ranked just below the emperor and living on a share of your kingdom’s taxes, while officials appointed by the emperor govern your lands.
tiers.kid: Han kings were usually relatives of the emperor, and they lived on taxes from the lands they were given.
tiers.rise: Kingdoms passed to the king’s eldest son by his queen, but from 127 BCE all a king’s sons were made marquesses with fiefs from his lands, so kingdoms shrank with each generation. A king who rebelled, or even murdered a slave, could lose his kingdom.
tiers.why: Below the emperor stood the kings, his brothers, uncles, nephews and sons other than the heir.

tiers.name: Officials and scholars
tiers.you: You have studied the Confucian classics and been recommended as filial and incorrupt; now you draw a salary in grain and coin and cannot be arrested without the emperor’s leave.
tiers.kid: Many Han officials studied the books of Confucius and were chosen for being good sons and honest men.
tiers.rise: A young man rose by study, a patron’s recommendation or service as a clerk in his commandery. Wealth could also buy office when the court sold posts, as it did on a large scale under Emperor Ling (168–189).
tiers.why: Those who served in government held a privileged place just below the nobles.

tiers.name: Great landed families
tiers.you: Your family owns wide fields worked by tenants who hand over half their harvest, keeps armed retainers, and sends its sons into office.
tiers.kid: Rich Han families owned large farms, and poorer families rented their fields and gave them about half the harvest.
tiers.rise: Families rose through office or trade and bought land with the profits. The court could resettle them or confiscate their estates, but by the late Western Han, Cho-yun Hsu argues, moving them by force had become unthinkable.
tiers.why: Below the officials, and often overlapping with them, stood the great landed families.

tiers.name: Farmers
tiers.you: You farm a few acres with your family, pay a poll tax in coin and a small share of your grain, and give the state a month’s labour every year; one day you may be sent to guard the frontier.
tiers.kid: Most people in Han China were farmers, and men had to work for the government for one month each year.
tiers.rise: Any free man could earn ranks of honour, granted on great occasions or bought with grain, that brought a better seat at village feasts, lighter punishments and relief from labour service. Study could carry a farmer’s son into office.
tiers.why: Farmers were the great majority and, in Confucian eyes, the “root” of the state, second only to scholars.

tiers.name: Artisans
tiers.you: You cast mirrors or lacquer cups in a workshop, may wear silk and ride a horse as no registered merchant may, and earn well if you become a master of your craft.
tiers.kid: Han craftspeople made shiny lacquer cups, bronze mirrors and fine silk cloth.
tiers.rise: Skill could make an artisan prosperous, and no law kept him from office, though few took that path: one painter who worked at the Imperial Academy turned down repeated nominations.
tiers.why: Artisans stood between farmers and merchants in the Confucian order.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You may grow richer than a marquess trading salt, iron or silk, but as a registered merchant you must wear white, pay a double poll tax and may never hold office.
tiers.kid: Some Han merchants grew very rich, but laws kept many of them from wearing silk or working for the government.
tiers.rise: Merchants bought land with their profits despite the bans, and a few entered office when the court needed their skills, as under Emperor Wu, though an edict of 7 BCE again barred them from the bureaucracy.
tiers.why: Merchants came last of the four occupations, scorned by scholars as parasites, yet many were rich.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You belong to a master who pays a tax on you each year; he may beat you but may not kill you, your children will be born slaves, and only your master or the emperor can set you free.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; in Han China there were few of them.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by the emperor’s grant, a master’s choice or purchase. In one exceptional case the former slave Jin Midi rose to be one of the regents of the empire.
tiers.why: Slaves (nubi) were few, perhaps one person in a hundred, far fewer than in the Roman world.
